summary: Intermittent throughput lull: NVMe IO-wait + tenant-heartbeat suppression causing autoscaler blindspot
description:
Issue summary:
Customer AtlasDocs reported three short (~2-6 minute) windows of degraded throughput and elevated p99 on several reserved routes during peak traffic on 2025-11-09. Symptoms: increased per-request GPU wait time, queued batches growing, autoscaler did not add capacity during windows.

Impact:
- Customer sees 20-40% drop in sustained throughput for routed endpoints (p50 OK, p99 degraded).
- Some streaming requests disconnected and fell back to hosted fallback model.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (us-east), reserved tenant for AtlasDocs (dedicated instance id: dp-us-east-47).
- Models impacted: llama-70b-quant-v2 and chat-medium-v1.

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Traffic ramp to peak (~300 RPS sustained for 2-5 min).
2) Background checkpointing workload on co-located tenant triggers large NVMe writes.
3) Serving hosts report storage IO wait spikes and increased GPU io-wait times.
4) Heartbeat metric aggregation for tenant becomes sparse (suppressed by short-lived heartbeat jitter).
5) Autoscaler telemetry filter discards window; no scale-up occurs.

Logs (excerpt):
- kernel: nvme0n1: io 12345 queued, io_wait=1200ms
- serving-runtime: gpu-attach-delay=850ms (p99), batch_queue_depth=42
- autoscaler: telemetry_window=2025-11-09T17:03:00Z samples=2 (threshold samples<3 -> skip)
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Send sustained traffic to dedicated tenant at peak RPS. 2) Start a small background write-heavy job on one co-located node (checkpoint writer). 3) Observe NVMe io-wait spikes on that node and elevated gpu-attach-delay in serving-runtime metrics. 4) Check autoscaler logs for telemetry window drop and skipped scale-up.
logs: kernel: nvme0n1: io_wait=1234ms; serving-runtime: batch_enqueue_wait=220ms; allocator: hot_slots=18/32; autoscaler: window_skipped_due_to_low_samples=true; sidecar-checkpointer: active_writes=12; dstat: avg-wait=500ms
comments: 2025-11-09 17:15 Priya Shah: Customer reported first degraded window, provided /metrics snapshot and kernel logs. Escalated to Tier 2 SRE.
2025-11-09 18:02 Riley Chen: Observed NVMe io-wait spikes aligned with elevated batch_queue_depth. Autoscaler telemetry windows dropped to 1-2 samples during the spike.

2025-11-10 09:11 Marco Nguyen (Storage): Found GC-like write amplification events on NVMe device on host gnode-47-12 between 17:02-17:08. Triggered by repeated small checkpoint files from a background sidecar on tenant X.

2025-11-11 13:27 Evelyn Park (Platform): Reproduced locally with synthetic writer; when IO wait >800ms serving-runtime reports gpu-attach-delay and batchers stall. Filed allocator PR to avoid telemetry filtering on short windows (see PR linked).

2025-11-13 10:45 Riley Chen: Patch deployed to autoscaler to lower sample threshold for dedicated pools during peak windows; monitoring for recurrence. Notified customer of temporary mitigation steps.
investigation_notes:
- Correlation found between NVMe write bursts and serving-runtime gpu attach delays.
- Autoscaler logic previously required >=3 telemetry samples per window; short spikes with suppressed heartbeats produced 1-2 samples and the window was skipped, causing no scale-up.
- Root noisy tenant runs a sidecar checkpointer that writes many small files to local NVMe; combined with background kernel GC produced high io-wait.
- GPU slots were technically available but blocked waiting on PCIe/NVMe IO paths (io-wait manifests as gpu-attach-delay).
- Streaming clients that rely on continuous token emission timed out and took fallback routes.
hypothesis: High-frequency small writes from a co-located sidecar triggered NVMe internal maintenance/Garbage Collection leading to host-level IO wait. The heartbeat aggregator suppressed samples during jitter windows, and autoscaler ignored the short telemetry window. Together these caused apparent 'silent' GPU shortages and prevented automatic scaling.
findings:
- NVMe write pattern coincided with degraded throughput windows.
- Hosts with sidecar writer had p99 nvme wait >1s.
- Autoscaler logs show window_skipped flag and no scale_up attempts.
- After live mitigation (throttling sidecar writes) throughput recovered within 90-120s.
root_cause: Combination of storage-level IO amplification (small-file write pattern causing NVMe GC and elevated io-wait) and autoscaler telemetry filter that discarded short, sparse heartbeat windows. The suppressed telemetry created an autoscaler blindspot during short IO perturbations, so capacity was not added when needed.
workaround: Temporary options provided to customer: 1) Pin high-throughput routes to dedicated hosts using 'reserve_host' flag to isolate from noisy tenants. 2) Increase dedicated pool burst_capacity to allot headroom for short spikes. 3) Throttle sidecar/backup writers with local rate limiting (recommended immediate).
resolution_notes:
- Immediate: instructed AtlasDocs to throttle their sidecar checkpoint writes and applied node-level write-rate limiter on affected hosts.
- Mid-term: lowered autoscaler sample threshold for dedicated pools during peak windows (deployed 2025-11-12).
- Long-term: storage team will tune NVMe firmware heuristics and we will add a secondary telemetry path that hedges against heartbeat suppression (allocator PR #5321).
- Customer notified; monitoring set up for three 24-hour windows. No re-occurrence observed in 72h post-mitigation.
follow_up_actions: Storage: Engage vendor for NVMe GC firmware tuning (owner: Marco Nguyen)
Autoscaler: Add alternate heartbeat metric (owner: Riley Chen)
Platform: Add diagnostic alert for gpu-attach-delay > 500ms (owner: Evelyn Park)
Customer Success: Schedule postmortem call with AtlasDocs and share runbook for noisy-neighbor mitigation (owner: Priya Shah)
